title: Why gas spreads
hook: Molecules bounce at random. How likely is it that they all end up in one half?

knows: that a gas fills its container
that a fair coin lands heads half the time
doesNotKnow: that spreading out is a matter of counting arrangements, not a force

misconception: Gas molecules are pushed apart by a force to fill space.
objective: The learner can explain that each molecule is on either half by chance, so all 20 on one side has probability (1/2)^20, about 1 in a million, and that gases spread because spread-out arrangements vastly outnumber bunched ones.

claims.text: Each molecule of an ideal gas is on the left half 1 time in 2, independently of the others.
claims.source: Ideal gas, non-interacting molecules, uniform position distribution (Atkins, Physical Chemistry, statistical thermodynamics / entropy of expansion).

claims.text: The chance that all 20 are on the left at one instant is 1 in 1,048,576, about one in a million.
No force pushes the gas apart; there are vastly more spread-out arrangements than bunched ones.
claims.source: Statistical interpretation of entropy, S = k ln W; free expansion of an ideal gas involves no intermolecular force (Atkins, Physical Chemistry, 'the statistical entropy').

claims.text: A real sample of gas holds about 10²³ molecules or more.
claims.source: Avogadro constant 6.022 × 10²³ per mole (CODATA); a mole of gas at room conditions fills about 24 L.

claims.text: Stage: each button takes 1,000 independent snapshots from a seeded stream (seed 20, untuned); with 4 molecules about 62 of 1,000 are expected all-left.
claims.source: 1000/16 = 62.5 expected for 4; 1000/1024 ≈ 1 for 10; 1000/2^20 ≈ 0.001 for 20. Real snapshots close in time are correlated; the model treats them as independent.

recall.question: 10 molecules in a box: the chance all are on the left half at one instant is about…
recall.why: (1/2)^10 = 1/1,024: each molecule is a coin flip, and all ten must land the same way.
